acts.head: Demand wobbles. Supplier orders wobble harder.
acts.sub: In a simulated four-tier chain, each customer's demand has a variation coefficient of 1.0. By the time orders reach the supplier, it's 1.94.

acts.head: Retailers won't hand over their sales data.
acts.sub: Bargaining power and competition rules keep it private. So each retailer forecasts on its own sales only, and passes its own noise upstream.

acts.head: Share only the market average.
acts.sub: Each retailer blends its own forecast 50/50 with the average demand of all four. Retailer order swings fall 18.6% and retailer costs 8%.

acts.head: The wholesaler pays a little for it.
acts.sub: Retailers now order in step, so wholesaler costs rise 1.4%. The chain still saves 0.4%, and retailers could pay upstream back and keep 20-43% of their gain.

endTitle: Share the average, not the data
endTag: Retailer costs fall 8% and wholesaler costs rise 1.4%, so the savings need sharing upstream.

post.linkedin:
In a new study, retailers cut costs 8% without showing anyone their own sales, by sharing only the market average. The catch sits one step upstream.

New open-access research in the International Journal of Production Economics, from authors at WU Vienna University of Economics and Business, simulates four retailers, a wholesaler, a manufacturer and a supplier. Normally each retailer forecasts on its own sales. Here they also get the average demand across all four, which encryption could compute without exposing anyone's numbers, and blend it 50/50 with their own forecast.

In the mid-variability scenario, retailer order swings fall 18.6% and retailer costs 8.0%. The whole chain saves 0.4%.

The trade-off: retailers now order in step, so the wholesaler sees bigger swings and pays 1.4% more. The authors suggest retailers pass part of the savings upstream; they would still keep 20-43% of them. It's a simulation with unlimited capacity, not a field test.

Would your retailers or distributors share a pooled demand signal if nobody saw their individual numbers?
